name: Gooseberry
lede: Gooseberry is a dark reddish purple from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary; the name is stranger than the fruit, since the common gooseberry colour name is a green.

sections.title: Not the green one
sections.body:
Paterson records gooseberry green as the yellowish green of the fruit, a colour name of the 1920s, also shortened to gooseberry [1]. The swatch here is far from that: it is a dark reddish purple, from Maerz and Paul's plate 55 [2]. The sources do not say which fruit Maerz and Paul had in mind, or whether they meant the fruit at all [2]. The ISCC-NBS system, in its 1955 terms, calls this swatch a dark reddish purple, a little under 4 units from its block center [2]. Compare [[plum]], [[mulberry]], [[aubergine]] and [[burgundy]].

One cochineal story belongs here. Greenfield reports that early-nineteenth-century English bakers used the dye to make apples and gooseberries blush as red as cherries and plums [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Only 24 of 23,781 archive paintings hold this color, rarer than 66 percent of named colors, and it most often plays a shadow in 50 percent of the 12 found by our inside-painting lens [4]. The earliest match is 1500, by Francisco de Osona, 430 years before the name's first record in our sources, 1930 [4]. As photographed, a dark purple match in a painting can be aged shadow glaze, not a pigment.

disambiguation.gloss: Paterson's gooseberry green is a yellowish green, unlike this purple
